label: Success and Failure
framing: Scripture refuses both the worship of success and the despair of failure. It measures a life not by the heights it reaches but by the faithfulness it keeps, and it tells the story of God working through the failed, the overlooked, and the ones who had to start again. Your worst chapter is not your verdict.
cultural: The honor-shame world of the Bible kept a brutal ledger of public standing, where to fail was to be shamed before the whole community and to rise was everything. Into that, Jesus blessed the poor and the meek, chose fishermen over the famous, and built his kingdom on a cross, which Rome read as the ultimate failure, scrambling every scale the world used to keep score.
historical: The desert fathers fled the applause of the city precisely because they saw how success corrodes the soul. Augustine, in the fifth century, traced his climb up the ladder of worldly success and named it a long flight from God, and the church has ever since warned that the world's victories can ruin a person more surely than its defeats.
application: Hold your ambitions with an open hand, pursuing excellence without making it your god. When you fail, grieve it honestly, learn what it has to teach, and then receive the mercy that does not depend on your record. Refuse the endless comparison that measures your life against the highlight reel of another's. And remember that the call is not to be successful but to be faithful, and that the two are not the same.

verses.text: And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the word that the Lord had spoken to him: “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times.” And he went outside and wept bitterly.
verses.where: As Peter denies Jesus a third time the rooster crows, the Lord turns and looks at him, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly. The site's note says only Luke records the look, and that Peter's tears come after it, not before. The plain note asks whether there is a failure you have stopped believing God could forgive, and says the bitter tears were not the end but the beginning of his turning.

verses.text: Jesus asked a third time, “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” Peter was deeply hurt that Jesus had asked him a third time, “Do you love Me?” “Lord, You know all things,” he replied. “You know I love You.” Jesus said to him, “Feed My sheep.
verses.where: Beside a charcoal fire the risen Jesus asks Peter a third time whether he loves him, and gives him his sheep to feed. The site's note says the three questions answer the three denials, and that the one who failed most publicly is given the care of the flock, because leadership in Christ's church rests on grace received, not on a record without failure. The plain note says Jesus did not ask him to explain himself or promise never to fail again; he asked one question and then gave him work.

verses.text: Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry.
verses.where: Near the end of his life Paul asks Timothy to bring Mark, because he is useful to him in the ministry. Years before, Paul had refused to take Mark with him because he had turned back, and the site's plain note says the list holds a man who left, a man who stayed and a man who came back. It asks whether there is someone you have written off whom God may have changed.

verses.text: “Master,” Simon replied, “we have worked hard all night without catching anything. But because You say so, I will let down the nets.”
verses.where: Simon tells Jesus that they have worked hard all night and caught nothing, and lets down the nets because Jesus says so. The site's note says Simon doubts the plan and obeys the person. The plain note says some have read the story as a promise of business success to those who obey, but it points the other way: the fishermen pull in the best catch of their lives and then leave it on the beach.

verses.text: His master replied, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master!’
verses.where: The master says to his servant, well done, good and faithful servant, you have been faithful with a few things. The site's note says the servant with two talents is praised word for word as the servant with five, because the master measures faithfulness, not quantity, which relieves those with lesser gifts of comparison and denies those with greater ones any boast. The plain note adds that the servant who failed was not the one with the least but the one who was afraid.

verses.text: Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful. I care very little, however, if I am judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. My conscience is clear, but that does not vindicate me. It is the Lord who judges me.
verses.where: Paul says stewards must be found faithful, and that he cares very little about being judged by the Corinthians or any human court, or even by himself, because the Lord judges him. The site's plain note asks whose verdict on you matters most: other people's, your own, or the Lord's. It adds that Paul's clear conscience does not clear him, which is a warning to leaders before it is a comfort.

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the wealthy man in his riches. But let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am the LORD, who exercises loving devotion, justice and righteousness on the earth— for I delight in these things,” declares the LORD.
verses.where: The LORD says the wise should not boast in their wisdom, nor the strong in their strength, nor the rich in their riches, but in understanding and knowing him. The site's note on the chapter says God names knowing him as the only thing worth boasting in. The three things people most often count as success are each set below it.

verses.text: Twelve months later, as he was walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon, the king exclaimed, “Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built by the might of my power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?” While the words were still in the king’s mouth, a voice came from heaven: “It is decreed to you, King Nebuchadnezzar, that the kingdom has departed from you.
verses.where: Walking on his palace roof, Nebuchadnezzar boasts of the great Babylon he has built by his own power for his own glory, and while the words are still in his mouth the sentence falls. The site's note on the chapter says that when his sanity returns he praises the King of heaven. Success that forgets where it came from is the most dangerous kind.

verses.text: But He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me. That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong.
verses.where: Paul pleads three times for his thorn to be removed and hears that God's grace is sufficient, for his power is perfected in weakness. The site's plain note calls it one man's honest witness that God sometimes answers a prayer for relief with grace to bear it, and asks where, in your weakness, you have known that grace to be enough for today. Paul ends by saying that when he is weak, then he is strong.

verses.text: But whatever was gain to me I count as loss for the sake of Christ. More than that, I count all things as loss compared to the surpassing excellence of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have lost all things. I consider them rubbish, that I may gain Christ and be found in Him, not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God on the basis of faith.
verses.where: Having listed his credentials, Paul says he counts everything he once gained as loss compared with knowing Christ and being found in him. The site's plain note suggests making your own list, your background, achievements and good record, and asking which you lean on to feel right with God. They are counted as loss not because they are bad but because he is better.

misread.taken: Though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up is quoted as a promise that a good person always bounces back, so that someone who does not recover from a failure must not be righteous, or not trying hard enough.
misread.says: The site's note says it is a proverb, describing how life usually goes under God and not a promise for every case. Seven is a number of fullness, so its point is resilience: the righteous are knocked down again and again and are not finished, because God upholds them. The note adds that Job, Ecclesiastes and the lament psalms speak honestly of righteous people who suffer long without visible recovery, and that the New Testament places the final rising of the righteous in the resurrection.
misread.text: For though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up; but the wicked stumble in bad times.

whole: If a failure has left you in a dark place, with thoughts of hurting yourself or weeks of lost sleep and hope, tell someone you trust today, a doctor, a pastor or a friend, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Failure comes in many forms: a business that went under, an exam failed twice, a marriage that ended, a ministry that collapsed, a moral fall that everyone now knows about, or simply the sense of having let everyone down. Success has its own troubles, less often admitted: the fear of losing it, the emptiness after the goal is reached, the way it can quietly take God's place. Many people carry both, measuring their worth against a scoreboard that never stops changing.

Scripture is full of people who failed, and it does not hide them. Peter denied Jesus three times by a fire. Mark turned back partway through the work, and Paul refused to take him again. Simon worked all night and caught nothing. It is just as honest about success: Nebuchadnezzar boasted over the city he had built, and the sentence fell while the words were in his mouth. What the Bible questions is the scoreboard itself. Jeremiah sets wisdom, strength and riches below knowing God, and Paul counts his whole impressive record as loss beside Christ. The master in Jesus' parable praises the servant with two talents in exactly the words he uses for the servant with five. Both the despair of failure and the pride of success rest on the same mistake, that a person is what they achieve.

So the Bible's wisdom does not tell you to stop caring about your work or to pretend a failure did not matter. Peter wept bitterly, and that was right. It tells you to bring the failure to the Lord who already sees it, to own what was yours and learn what it teaches, and to receive the mercy that does not depend on your record. It asks whose verdict matters most, and Paul's answer is neither the crowd's nor his own but the Lord's. In success it asks for thanks and an open hand, remembering where the strength came from. In failure it asks you to let the next small faithful task be enough for today, as Peter was given sheep to feed. And it asks the church to be the kind of place where Mark can come back.

The hope Scripture gives is that a failure is not a final verdict. The Lord who turned and looked at Peter had already prayed for him, and the man who denied him by one fire was restored by another. Mark, written off, was useful again. Paul heard that grace is sufficient and power is perfected in weakness. Whatever the scoreboard says about you this year, the one who measures faithfulness and not quantity is the one who will say the last word, and he has a habit of handing work back to people who thought they had lost it for good.
deep.sit: Whose verdict on your life have you been living under, and what would it mean to let the Lord's be the last word?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says the psalm does not end by giving the doubter what others had but by giving him God. Pray verse 25 slowly, and ask him to make it true of you.
prayer.text: Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand. You guide me with Your counsel, and later receive me in glory. Whom have I in heaven but You? And on earth I desire no one besides You. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.

careLines.text: If you are in a dark place now, you do not have to pretend to be strong, and you do not have to carry it alone.
Seeking help is not a failure of faith.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
